title: Segregation in Long Branch and New York theatres
summary: Crouch asks about integration in Long Branch; Greer says it was like Georgia and tells of his wife being sent to the balcony.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Let me get a little bit more information about your home town. Apparently you growing up in Long Branch, there was a lot of integration going on.
I mean there was more mixing of black people and white people.
Naw, Long Branch the same as was/ Georgia.

If you went to the theatre, you had to sit up in the balcony. New York was the same way. 105th Street, I went into Child's and we could take it out, but you ain't going to sit down and eat. In New York. My wife -- my wife was a very famous dancer,

too, you know. I took her to the theatre -- wasn't the Apollo, it's still up there, bought a ticket, highest price ticket to go and see a movie, walk in and the usher tell me, 'Upstairs.' I say, 'No, these kind are for downstairs.' He said, 'Colored people go upstairs.' I said, 'All right', went back and said, 'Give me my money.' He said, 'what's the matter?' 'I pay you my money for orchestra seats, you going to send me upstairs? I don't climb no stairs. Just give me my money, let's have it nice and peaceful. Give me my money.' So she did me and my wife.

My wife, when I was on the road, my wife and her mother, they went down to visit my people and she went to the same theatre, they all went to see Peggy play at Long Branch, to go sit in the gallery. Now, in the meantime, -- you want to stay in New York --
